newsitem.title: FRANCE: Leaked French budget numbers disappoint economists.
newsitem.headline: Leaked French budget numbers disappoint economists.

text.p: France's 1997 budget will produce the deficit number needed to qualify for European monetary union but the final central government deficit is higher than most had expected and is disappointing, economists said on Wednesday.

"This budget overall looks broadly credible, though the numbers themselves are not looking too good. Analysis based purely on the numbers would say they've not done too much at all," said economist Sean Shepley at CS First Boston.
Figures leaked by the government to several newspapers and reported on Wednesday put the central government deficit at 283.6 billion francs, versus the 288 billion forecast for 1996.
"It looks to me as though this is a budget which achieves a cut in the deficit level primarily by a number of accounting measures," Shepley added.

Newspapers reported that the government intended to cut its public deficit in 1997 to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and that the central government deficit to be officially presented later in the day would be 283.6 billion francs, well above the government target of less than 250 billion.
"It's quite disappointing, this smaller-than-expected cut in the central government deficit - it will be 3.5 percent of GDP in 1997," said JP Morgan economist David Naude.
"This doesn't mean total deficits can't be brought down to three percent but it does mean they have to find half a point of GDP elsewhere," he added.

"The interesting point is that the government is saying it is being conservative to the extent that it is not looking for cuts it would not be able to deliver. But in reality it's being conservative because they're facing a shortfall in revenue," said Naude.
"Basically, it tells you that even preliminary to the 1997 plan there is a problem for this year," he added.
The papers reported that the budget was keeping a commitment of freezing central government spending at the 1996 level, which is expected to be 1,552.9 billion francs.

Daily Le Figaro said debt charges for the government would rise from 226 billion in 1996 to 245 billion in 1997 that civil service pay would climb by 1.7 percent. Spending cuts would be more than 60 billion francs and government spending would rise by 1.5 percent next year.
The government's budget projects that receipts will rise by 2.0 percent next year, Le Figaro said.

Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley, said of the 284 billion central government deficit figure: "If it's true, it's a bit surprising. I'd prefer to wait for the budget itself but I don't like what I read in the papers."
On the plus side, the government looked like it was trying to be transparent, he said, even though the budget was "much softer" than was expected three to four months ago.
Most importantly, Germany is looking for evidence that France is cutting its budget deficits by structural reform.
"My worry is, it looks possible there'll be a quality gap between the German and French fiscal packages," Chaney said.
To get total public deficits to three percent or less of GDP next year, the government is banking on spending cuts.
The central government budget figure of 283.6 billion after 25 billion francs of tax cuts is only about four billion less than the forecast 1996 deficit.

Among other things, the government is set to include funds transferred from France Telecom -- 37.5 billion francs is being handed over to cover future pension liability at France Telecom -- to make the Maastricht deficit mathematics works out.
An accounting surplus from the CADES welfare debt repayment fund and a surplus in the national unemployment fund UNEDIC are also being counted on.

Sizing up market reaction, Credit Lyonnais bank senior bond analyst Iain Lindsay said: "The market has already got the good news and the risk is on the downside. It won't be major but the market has been too optimistic and 283 is not a great number."

Shepley at CS First Boston and Lindsay at Credit Lyonnais both said the Bank of France could still cut the intervention rate by 10 basis points on Thursday, while David Naude at JP Morgan said the central bank would most likely hold off.
-- Brian Love, Paris Newsroom +33 1 4221 5452
